question: For a classification task with a softmax output layer, the natural loss function is:
explanation: Softmax + cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of a categorical distribution — the right pairing both numerically (clean gradients) and statistically (proper scoring rule).

question: Why is *mean squared error* a poor loss for classification probabilities?
options: Its gradient is small when the model is very confidently wrong, slowing learning
It is mathematically equivalent to cross-entropy
explanation: Plot d/dp of (p − 1)²: tiny near p ≈ 0 (confidently-wrong region). Cross-entropy's gradient is 1 − p there, so it punishes confident mistakes hard.

question: Cross-entropy between target distribution p and model q is H(p, q) = −Σ p(x) log q(x). It equals H(p) + KL(p ‖ q). What does this tell you?
options: Minimizing cross-entropy w.r.t. q is equivalent to minimizing KL(p ‖ q), since H(p) is constant w.r.t. q
Cross-entropy is always less than or equal to entropy
KL divergence is symmetric in its arguments
Cross-entropy and entropy are the same when p = q
explanation: When you train on fixed targets, H(p) is a constant, so minimizing cross-entropy *is* minimizing KL — pulling the model distribution toward the data distribution.

question: L1 loss (mean absolute error) is more *robust to outliers* than L2 (squared error) because:
options: L1 grows linearly with the residual instead of quadratically, so a single huge error doesn't dominate the gradient
L1 is always smaller than L2
L1 is differentiable everywhere; L2 is not
L1 has a closed-form minimum; L2 doesn't
explanation: Outliers drive L2 to chase them because the gradient scales with the residual. L1's gradient is just ±1 — every example contributes equally to the update direction. Huber loss is the standard compromise.
